questions.question_text: A buyer and seller sign the purchase and sale agreement on Friday. By when must the brokerage firm place the earnest money in its trust account?
questions.correct_answer: Within 5 banking days after both parties execute the P&S
distractors: Within 3 banking days after both parties execute the P&S
Within 10 calendar days after both parties execute the P&S
By the next business day
questions.explanation: Commission Rule 4.7(b): all deposits held as escrow agent under a purchase and sale agreement must be deposited in the firm's trust or escrow account not later than five banking days after the P&S agreement is executed by both seller and buyer. 26 V.S.A. § 2214(a) sets the same five-banking-day standard.

questions.question_text: Where must Vermont brokers hold earnest money deposits?
questions.correct_answer: A trust account at a VT-licensed bank
distractors: The broker's general business account
Any FDIC-insured bank nationwide
A personal savings account at any bank
questions.explanation: Every brokerage firm holding funds of others must maintain a pooled interest-bearing trust account in a bank or other regulated financial institution licensed in Vermont (Rule 4.7(a)). Interest on the pooled account is remitted to the Vermont Housing Finance Agency under 26 V.S.A. § 2214 — no earnings may be made available to the firm or its licensees.

questions.question_text: A broker receives earnest money on Wednesday. She plans to deposit it into her office operating account temporarily. Is this permitted?
questions.correct_answer: No, it must go into a trust account
distractors: Yes, if deposited within 5 banking days
Yes, if the buyer consents in writing
Yes, for up to 72 hours only
questions.explanation: Earnest money must be deposited into a designated trust or escrow account that is separate from the broker's personal and office operating accounts. Placing client funds into an operating account, even temporarily, violates Vermont trust account requirements.

questions.question_text: Which of the following accounts may hold client earnest money in Vermont?
questions.correct_answer: A designated escrow account at a VT bank
distractors: The broker's personal checking account
A money market fund at an out-of-state bank
The listing agent's business account
questions.explanation: Client earnest money must be held in the brokerage firm's pooled interest-bearing trust or escrow account at a bank or other regulated financial institution licensed in Vermont (Rule 4.7(a)). Personal accounts, operating accounts, and out-of-state institutions do not qualify.

questions.question_text: A brokerage firm deposits earnest money on the seventh banking day after the purchase and sale agreement was signed by both parties. What is the regulatory consequence?
questions.correct_answer: The firm violated the 5-banking-day deposit rule
distractors: No violation if the check clears successfully
A warning is issued only for first offenses
The deposit is valid if both parties agree
questions.explanation: The deposit is due within five banking days of execution of the purchase and sale agreement by both parties (Rule 4.7(b); 26 V.S.A. § 2214(a)). Depositing on day seven is late regardless of whether the check clears, and failure to comply with § 2214 is unprofessional conduct under 26 V.S.A. § 2296(2).

questions.question_text: A Vermont brokerage firm deposits a small amount of its own money into the client trust account solely to cover bank service charges and keep the account above the minimum balance. Is this permitted?
distractors: No, any firm money in a trust account is commingling
No, unless the Commission approves in advance
No, unless every client consents in writing
questions.explanation: A brokerage firm may deposit its own funds in the trust account to cover bank service charges or to meet a minimum balance that avoids them, and the nominal sums needed to keep the account open are excepted from the commingling ban (Rule 4.7(i); 26 V.S.A. § 2296(1)). What the firm may NOT do is deplete the principal trust funds; specialized charges such as check printing, wire fees, and overdrafts are the firm's business expense.

questions.question_text: When may the Vermont Real Estate Commission inspect a broker's trust account records?
questions.correct_answer: At any time during business hours
distractors: Only with 30 days advance notice
Only upon receiving a formal complaint
Only during annual audits
questions.explanation: The firm's records — including the trust account records itemized in Rule 4.7(g) — must be available to the Commission and its agents during regular business hours, with no advance notice required (Rule 4.14).

questions.question_text: What does commingling mean in Vermont real estate practice?
questions.correct_answer: Mixing client trust funds with broker funds
distractors: Sharing a listing with another brokerage
Combining two buyer deposits in one check
Using one trust account for multiple clients
questions.explanation: Commingling is mixing client trust funds with the brokerage firm's or licensee's own funds — prohibited by 26 V.S.A. § 2296(1). A single pooled trust account holding several clients' deposits is not commingling; Rule 4.7(a) actually requires the firm to maintain a pooled account.

questions.question_text: A Commission investigator arrives at a brokerage at 10 AM on Tuesday to review trust records. The broker says he needs a week to prepare. What should happen?
questions.correct_answer: The broker must allow immediate access
distractors: The investigator must return in one week
The broker can request a 48-hour delay
The investigator needs a court order first
questions.explanation: Under Rule 4.14(b) the principal broker, broker in charge, or a designee must cooperate in good faith with a Commission inspection during regular business hours and may remain present — but the Commission's agent may not be denied access to the records, even if no one is available to sit in.

questions.question_text: A broker pays her office rent directly from the client trust account, intending to replace the funds tomorrow. This practice is:
distractors: Acceptable if funds are replaced promptly
Permitted for amounts under $2,000
Allowed with written client approval
questions.explanation: Using client trust funds for a business expense is commingling and conversion, regardless of intent to repay. Rule 4.7(i) permits only the firm's own money to go IN to cover bank service charges; nothing permits trust money to come OUT for the firm's benefit, and Rule 4.7(i) forbids depleting the principal.

questions.question_text: A buyer's deposit is reasonably expected to earn more than $100 in interest. What does Vermont require?
questions.correct_answer: Move it to an individual interest-bearing account if the depositor requests
distractors: Move it to an individual account automatically, with no request needed
Remit the interest to the Real Estate Commission
Return the interest to the brokerage firm as a service fee
questions.explanation: A deposit reasonably expected to earn more than $100 must be placed in an individual interest-bearing trust account if the person making the deposit requests it, identifying the SSN or TIN of the person entitled to the interest (Rule 4.7(c)). Deposits not expected to earn more than $100 stay in the firm's pooled account, whose interest goes to the Vermont Housing Finance Agency (26 V.S.A. § 2214).

questions.question_text: A client asks whether her deposit will earn interest. What must the broker disclose?
questions.correct_answer: Whether it earns interest and who gets it
distractors: Only the current interest rate offered
Only the bank name and account number
Nothing unless the client asks in writing
questions.explanation: The broker must inform the depositor whether the funds are deposited into an individual interest-bearing account or the firm's pooled account, and who is entitled to the interest (26 V.S.A. § 2214). Under Rule 4.7(f), interest on an individual account is paid out to the person entitled to it at the same time as the principal.

questions.question_text: What written document must the broker retain regarding trust account interest disclosure?
questions.correct_answer: A signed disclosure from the beneficial owner
distractors: A bank-issued certificate of deposit
A Commission letter approving the account
A notarized affidavit filed with the court
questions.explanation: The broker must retain a written statement of this disclosure signed by the beneficial owner — the person whose funds are being held — confirming they were told whether the account is individual or pooled and who receives the interest (26 V.S.A. § 2214).

questions.question_text: A broker holds deposits from multiple clients in one pooled trust account. What must each depositor be told?
questions.correct_answer: That their funds are in a pooled account
distractors: The names of all other depositors
The total balance of the pooled account
Nothing, pooled accounts need no disclosure
questions.explanation: Under 26 V.S.A. § 2214 the broker must inform each depositor whether their funds sit in an individual interest-bearing account or the firm's pooled account, and retain that disclosure signed by the beneficial owner. Pooled-account interest is remitted to the Vermont Housing Finance Agency, not paid to the depositor or the firm.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is NOT required in Vermont trust account disclosure?
questions.correct_answer: The projected interest earnings for the year
distractors: Whether the account is interest-bearing
Who receives the interest earned
Whether funds are in an individual or pooled account
questions.explanation: The disclosure must cover whether the account is interest-bearing, who is entitled to the interest, and whether funds are individual or pooled — signed by the beneficial owner (26 V.S.A. § 2214). Projected annual earnings are not a required disclosure item.
